classroom_exchanges.question: Can a field return to the same value?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: Yes. There is no obstruction, just as a particle coordinate may return to an earlier value.

classroom_exchanges.question: Why speak of spacetime events or a trajectory when the boundary data are field values?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: The trajectory becomes a field history, and each boundary datum is the whole field on a selected time slice.

classroom_exchanges.question: Is the exponential connected to multiplying successive small-step amplitudes?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: Yes; successive step factors multiply.

classroom_exchanges.question: Is the path sum itself the probability?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: No. It is a complex probability amplitude; multiplying it by its complex conjugate gives the probability.

classroom_exchanges.question: How can infinitely many unit-magnitude contributions converge, and are they being minimized?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: They are summed, not minimized. Their oscillatory phases cancel, while paths near stationary action cancel least.

classroom_exchanges.question: Does the exponential require an ℏ?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: Yes; ℏ belongs in the exponent, although it may later be set to one.

classroom_exchanges.question: Are field quanta necessarily identifiable as particles?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: Not always in the conventional observable sense. Confined quarks are the main example discussed; the field-particle correspondence and terminology depend on context.

classroom_exchanges.question: Must field histories be continuous or approximately continuous?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: No. All lattice field assignments are included, and quantum fields fluctuate strongly.

classroom_exchanges.question: Are fields and their derivatives assigned independently?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: No. Field values are assigned; derivatives are reconstructed from neighboring differences.

classroom_exchanges.question: Can the field-value range also be discretized, and what happens with several fields?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: The value range may be divided into intervals, and every field receives a value at every site.

classroom_exchanges.question: Must complex-valued field histories obey the smoothness conditions of analytic functions?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: No. Complex-valued does not mean analytic; typical histories are not smooth.

classroom_exchanges.question: How does a computer know how many lattice assignments to sample or whether the calculation has converged?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: This is the developed subject of lattice quantum field theory, using methods related to statistical mechanics and checked through successful comparison with experiment.

classroom_exchanges.question: Do the Lagrangians under discussion contain second derivatives?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: No; the discussion is restricted to first-derivative theories.

classroom_exchanges.question: Does a one-link term contribute only when the relevant initial and final sites are adjacent?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: Yes, for that first-order neighboring-pair term.

classroom_exchanges.question: Must the second neighboring pair in a second-order term adjoin the first pair?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: No. Each factor independently sums over neighboring pairs; the pairs may share a site, remain separate, or coincide.

classroom_exchanges.question: Are there other two-step paths to the same diagonal endpoint?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: Yes. Both available two-step orderings contribute.

classroom_exchanges.question: Can a path traverse the same two cells repeatedly?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: Yes; repeated and backward traversals are allowed in the relativistic expansion.

classroom_exchanges.question: Do the factorials guarantee convergence?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: They ensure convergence of the exponential series but do not guarantee convergence of the separate sum over configurations.

classroom_exchanges.question: Could an electron and positron annihilate with no particles left?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: A no-output process violates energy conservation and cancels. Annihilation is possible when another field carries away the energy.

classroom_exchanges.question: Can the same process receive contributions from multiple histories?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: Yes. Its amplitude is the sum over every history joining the same initial and final states.

classroom_exchanges.question: Can four particles simply appear in the final state?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: That is a local operator reading, but the spacetime sum cancels it when energy cannot be conserved.

classroom_exchanges.question: Do energy and momentum conservation emerge from the calculation?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: Yes. Integration over time enforces energy conservation, and integration over space enforces momentum conservation.

classroom_exchanges.question: Can color theory be treated in the same way?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: Yes; it will be discussed later.

classroom_exchanges.question: Are the bottom and top of a Feynman diagram the initial and final particle configurations?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: Yes.

classroom_exchanges.question: Are coupling constants predicted by theory or determined experimentally?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: Symmetries sometimes relate them, but their numerical values generally come from experiment.

classroom_exchanges.question: Why be confident in the measured coupling constants?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: Once measured, changing them produces incorrect predictions.

classroom_exchanges.question: How many G_n-type interaction couplings govern electrons and photons?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: QED has one elementary interaction coupling, the electric charge, attached to the electron-electron-photon vertex.

classroom_exchanges.question: What about electron-proton scattering?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: In the elementary atomic treatment, the proton may be idealized as a fixed, infinitely heavy point source until its internal dynamics are included.

classroom_exchanges.question: Can the electron move nearly at light speed relative to the proton?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: Yes.

classroom_exchanges.question: Can the Higgs field replace the constant mass coefficient?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: Yes; that mechanism will be discussed.

classroom_exchanges.question: Can x and x′ represent neighboring points at different times?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: Yes; that is how vertical lattice propagation was represented.

classroom_exchanges.question: Which terms represent a particle standing still?
classroom_exchanges.answer_summary: The same-site squares from the finite difference and the mass term do so; the cross term represents motion.
